carryoverIn.title: Drift Harp
carryoverIn.pitch: A harp of plucked strings that you strum by dragging a finger or cursor across them, each string a Karplus-Strong plucked string tuned in pure just intonation and shown on a live fifths-and-thirds lattice. Play a looping chord progression and hear and see the pitch creep up by a syntonic comma (about a fifth of a semitone) every lap, a trick called a comma pump. A tempering dial lets you squeeze the drift shut and hear exactly what equal temperament trades away.
carryoverIn.whyNow: Timeless: a tuning-system explorer where the surprise is audible. The visitor discovers on their own that pure intervals do not close a loop, which most explainers only state in words.

research.summary: A comma pump is a repeating progression whose pure intervals almost, but not exactly, return to the start, so the pitch shifts by a small interval each lap. The standard case is the syntonic comma (81:80, about 21.5 cents) in the progression C G D A E C; both Wikipedia and the Xenharmonic Wiki describe it. A 5-limit just intonation lattice puts fifths (3/2) on one axis and major thirds (5/4) on the other, so a loop that does not close is the drift made visible. Karplus-Strong gives a cheap plucked string: a noise burst circulating in a delay line with an averaging filter, where loop length sets pitch and the filter sets decay. Browser Karplus-Strong demos exist (one was seen), which de-risks the sound engine, but none found combines it with a drifting lattice.

facts.claim: A comma pump is a progression that returns almost, but not exactly, to its starting pitch, shifting by a small interval each repetition; the classic syntonic example is C G D A E C, rising by 81:80 per lap in just intonation, and the pump closes exactly in 12-tone equal temperament (Wikipedia and Xenharmonic Wiki, as of 2026-10-12).
The syntonic comma is the ratio 81:80, about 21.5 cents, the gap between a Pythagorean ditone (81:64) and a just major third (5:4) (Xenharmonic Wiki and Wikipedia, as of 2026-10-12).

Karplus-Strong synthesis circulates a burst of noise through a delay line with an averaging low-pass filter; loop length sets pitch and the filter shapes decay, so high harmonics fade faster (Wikipedia, a Stanford explainer and the Csound manual, as of 2026-10-12).
A 5-limit pitch lattice puts just fifths (3/2) on one axis and just major thirds (5/4) on the other (Wikipedia Lattice article and Xenharmonic Wiki 5-limit entry, as of 2026-10-12).

inspirations: pitch lattice diagrams from xenharmonic tuning software

design.coreLoop: Drag across strings to strum, assemble a short loop of chords on the lattice, and let it cycle. Each lap the drift meter shows the pure tuning rising by one syntonic comma while a ghost of the starting pitch stays put. Turn the tempering dial to close the loop and hear what is lost, or chase a lap that lands back home using adaptive retuning. Every chord choice changes how fast and which way the pitch wanders, so there is always another loop to try.
sophisticationHooks: Karplus-Strong voices with per-string damping, pick position and a stroke-speed-dependent excitation, polyphonic across a harp of 12 strings
Live 5-limit pitch lattice with ratio and cents readouts; the drift is the distance between where a loop starts and where it ends on the lattice
Tempering dial that continuously morphs pure ratios toward 12-tone equal temperament, with a seeded generative drone that makes beating audible
Shareable URL hash holding the chord loop, tempering amount and seed

Build: Karplus-Strong plucks rendered on demand into AudioBuffers in the main thread (no AudioWorklet, so no CSP issue) with a voice pool, 12 strings, canvas harp and lattice views, pointer/touch strum and keyboard play, loop editor with 6 slots, drift meter with a ghost of the starting pitch, tempering dial, a muted-state visual story (lattice path, cents readout), URL-hash share, about panel. The pump claim is solid, but the audible effect depends on voice-leading that keeps every chord pure; the spec fixes four tested loops, including the C G D A E C case, and checks the lap drift numerically in a unit test.

ideas.title: Historical Date Converter
ideas.plainSentence: A converter that lets you turn a date from the Julian or Gregorian calendar into the other, by country, and flags dates that never existed.
ideas.pitch: Pick a date between 1500 and 1930 and a place, and the page shows what that day was called under the old Julian calendar and the modern Gregorian one, with the weekday, the day count and a clear flag when the date was skipped there. It opens on today's date in 1582, a day that did not exist in Rome, so the first result is a surprise. Genealogists, history writers and curious people get a private, offline answer with the working shown step by step.
ideas.firstMinute: The page opens with 13 October 1582 in Rome already entered and the result on screen: that date never existed there, the calendar jumped from Thursday 4 October to Friday 15 October, and the same day in England was 3 October. One button swaps in any other date or place, so the visitor gets a first success without reading anything.
conceptsToLearn: A calendar date can name different days depending on which calendar a country was using at the time.
ideas.whyNow: Today is 13 October, a date inside the ten days (5 to 14 October 1582) that were skipped in Rome, Spain and Portugal. The topic is timeless for anyone reading old letters, parish records or diaries.

purposeDetail.job: Convert a historical date between the Julian and Gregorian calendars using the switch date of the chosen country, and say when the date was skipped or ambiguous.
purposeDetail.audience: Family-history researchers, history students, writers and anyone reading old documents, letters or diaries dated before their country changed calendars.
purposeDetail.freeGap: Free Julian-to-Gregorian converters and old-style/new-style converters already exist, so no paywall is claimed. The remaining gap is one page that is private and offline, knows each region's own switch date, flags skipped dates and the old 25 March New Year, and shows every step of its arithmetic.
purposeDetail.oracle: Julian day numbers (2299160 for 4 October 1582 Julian and 2299161 for 15 October 1582 Gregorian, from the IDL documentation example and the Julian day reference), the Gregorian leap rule from the Naval Observatory and a calendar FAQ, and the published skips: 4 to 15 October 1582 in Rome and 2 to 14 September 1752 in Britain (the Act's text). Further cases are computed per the leap rule and labelled computed.
purposeDetail.inputs: A year, month and day, plus a region from a bundled list of about 20 places with their switch dates, and an optional choice of which calendar the date was written in.
purposeDetail.outputs: The date in both calendars, the weekday, the Julian Day Number, a dual-date form such as 1731/32 for dates before the New Year moved, a skipped-date warning, and days between two dates across a switch. Results can be copied as text.
purposeDetail.limits: Switch dates varied inside some countries (German states, Swiss cantons, colonies); the page uses one date per region and says so. It does not handle non-Christian calendars, and it is not legal or genealogical proof.

research.summary: Verified by search only (no page opened). The 1582 jump from 4 to 15 October is confirmed by day-count documentation, a reference article and a genealogy magazine; Britain's 2 to 14 September 1752 jump and the move of New Year to 1 January are confirmed by the Act itself and a magazine article. The leap rule matches the Naval Observatory's FAQ and a calendar FAQ. The riots over lost days in 1752 are called a largely later myth by a historian and a second site. Russia 1918 and Greece (1923 or 1924, tables differ) are single-table claims and stay unverified; Sweden was not confirmed and is left out.

facts.claim: In 1582 the Catholic countries that adopted the reform at once (Rome and most of Italy among them) went from Thursday 4 October straight to Friday 15 October, so 5 to 14 October 1582 do not exist there.

Britain and its colonies moved to the Gregorian calendar by the Calendar (New Style) Act 1750 so that Wednesday 2 September 1752 was followed by Thursday 14 September 1752, and New Year's Day moved from 25 March to 1 January.
Oracle: the day count is continuous across the 1582 switch; Julian day number 2299160 is 4 October 1582 (Julian) and 2299161 is 15 October 1582 (Gregorian).

Gregorian rule: a year is a leap year if divisible by 4, except century years not divisible by 400, giving 97 leap years per 400 years and an average year of 365.2425 days; the Julian average of 365.25 days gains about 3 days per 400 years.
Historians treat the story of 1752 mobs demanding their eleven days back as largely a later myth; the slogan is tied to a banner in a 1755 painting about the 1754 Oxfordshire election.

As of 2026-10-13, per one table only: Russia moved after 31 January 1918 and Greece changed in 1923 (another table gives 1924). Not confirmed by two separate results, so the page shows these rows as reported or leaves them out.

ideas.title: Sealed-Bid Auction Lesson
ideas.plainSentence: A lesson that lets you bid against simulated rivals in first-price and second-price sealed auctions and see how shading your bid changes your profit.
ideas.pitch: You get a private value for an item (say a mug worth 60 play-dollars to you) and bid against four simulated rivals, first in a rising-price auction, then in sealed first-price and second-price versions. A slider shades your bid below or above your value and a profit curve, built from thousands of replayed rounds, shows that shading pays in the first-price auction and never pays in the second-price one. You leave knowing why the rule of the game, not good manners, makes honest bidding the best plan, and exactly when that stops being true.
ideas.firstMinute: The first frame already shows an ascending auction running: a price ladder climbs, rivals drop out, and a card says what the item is worth to you. You tap Drop out when the price reaches your value, see you won with a small profit, and see the same round replayed with a higher and a lower dropout point so you can see why leaving at your value was best.
conceptsToLearn: your value for an item is what it is worth to you; profit is value minus the price you pay
ideas.whyNow: Timeless. The ad-tech industry's 2019 switch from second-price to first-price auctions (per two trade reports) made bid shading a live topic, and this lesson shows the arithmetic behind it.

purposeDetail.concept: In a sealed-bid second-price auction the highest bidder wins but pays the second-highest bid, so your own bid only decides whether you win, never what you pay; bidding your true value is therefore a dominant strategy when values are private. In a first-price auction you pay what you bid, so you shade below value; with n risk-neutral bidders (n counts you) whose values are independent and uniform on 0 to 1, the equilibrium bid is (n-1)/n of your value.
purposeDetail.whyNiche: It is usually taught as a theorem or as a one-line conclusion, so it sounds like an opinion. Few places let a learner try to cheat the rule and watch it fail, or show that the same honest bid is wrong under a different rule.
purposeDetail.audience: Curious adults, students of economics or computer science, and anyone who has argued about eBay, ad markets or spectrum sales.
prerequisites: subtracting a price from a value
misconceptions: In a sealed second-price auction, bidding above my value helps me win more, so it is worth it.
Shading my bid below value is always the smart move, whatever the auction rule.
purposeDetail.ahaMoment: Fix the rivals' bids in a single round and drag your bid anywhere above the highest rival bid: in the second-price auction the price you pay never moves. Then run the replay: the average-profit curve peaks exactly at your value, while the first-price curve peaks lower, at four fifths of value with four rivals.
demos: Rung 1: a rising-price ladder auction with four simulated rivals; you choose when to drop out; the page replays the round with other dropout points.

Rung 2: sealed first-price round; type or drag a bid; the winner pays their own bid; a few single rounds, then a 5000-round replay shows average profit against bid as a fraction of value, peaking at the shaded point (n-1)/n.
Rung 3: sealed second-price round with the same slider; the profit curve now peaks exactly at honest bidding, and the page marks the winning-and-paying breakdown for any bid you choose.
Rung 4: what-if panel: change the number of rivals and watch the first-price best shade move toward honesty while second-price stays at honest.

Rung 5: break the guarantee: switch to pay-your-bid pricing, or add a seller who places a fake bid just under yours; honest bidding stops being best, shown by the page's own arithmetic from the stated rules. Interdependent values appear only as a short static worked example.

Rung 6: real world card: a large ad exchange moved from second-price to first-price auctions in 2019, per two trade reports, and buyers added bid shading; the rules changed the behaviour. No brand name or logo on the page.
checkQuestions: Your value is 60 and the highest rival bids 45. You bid 50 in a second-price auction. What do you pay? (45)
Same values, first-price auction, you bid 50 and the highest rival bids 45 so you win. What is your profit? (10)
With 4 bidders in all (you included) with values spread evenly from 0 to 1, what share of your value should you bid in a first-price auction? (three quarters)
Name one change to the rules that stops honest bidding being best in a second-price auction.

research.summary: University course notes agree that truthful bidding is a dominant strategy in the second-price sealed-bid auction and that bidding (n-1)/n of value, with n counting every bidder including you, is the symmetric equilibrium of the first-price auction for independent uniform values; both were found again on 2026-10-13 in separate courses. Lab studies are reported to show people overbid in the sealed second-price format; that rising-price formats are learned faster is reported but could not be tied to one result today. The equivalence of the rising-price auction and the second-price auction holds for private values per one handbook page only. Google's move to first-price auctions in 2019 (AdExchanger, PPC Land) is a live example of rules reshaping behaviour. The Ausubel and Milgrom paper and the two Toronto lectures from the scout were not found again and are not used.

facts.claim: In a sealed-bid second-price auction the highest bidder wins and pays the second-highest bid, and bidding your true value is a dominant strategy under private values (Brown and McGill course notes, as of 2026-10-13).

In a first-price sealed-bid auction with n risk-neutral bidders (you included) whose values are independent and uniform on 0 to 1, bidding (n-1)/n of your value is the symmetric equilibrium (Brown course notes and a calculator page, with a second Brown course and an arXiv paper consistent; as of 2026-10-13).

Lab experiments find people often bid above value in sealed second-price auctions, missing the dominant strategy, and the overbidding persists with experience (Berlin School of Economics summary and a UTS re-analysis, as of 2026-10-13).

Reported, per one handbook page (unconfirmed): under independent private values the rising-price auction and the sealed second-price auction share the same optimal strategy; the equivalence is said not to hold for interdependent values with more than two bidders.

Reported, not confirmed (summary of a citing paper, source result not identified): the same lab literature says people find the dominant strategy quickly in the rising-price format while overbidding persists in the sealed format.

risks: Honest bidding is best under the second-price rule with private values and independent bidders; the rising-price auction shares that strategy under private values, which rests on one handbook page, so the page shows that line as reported, per that page.

Equilibrium shading (n-1)/n holds only for risk-neutral bidders with independent uniform values and n counts you; with four rivals n is 5 and the best shade is four fifths. The page states the assumptions and labels rival behaviour as simulated, play money only.

The claim that people learn the dominant strategy quickly in the rising-price format could not be tied to one result today; it is shown as reported or omitted, and the ladder rung is justified by the page's own demonstration, not by that claim.
The seller-fake-bid and pay-your-bid demos are the page's own arithmetic from stated rules, not sourced claims about real markets; labelled as models.
Outlets disagree on the exact start of the 2019 rollout; the page says 'in 2019, per AdExchanger and PPC Land' and no more precise date, and uses no company logo or brand styling.

The scout's Ausubel and Milgrom claim (the Vickrey format is rare in practice) and the revenue-equivalence claim were not found again and are not used; revenue equivalence may appear only as the simulation's own output.

Check question wording must name that you win; the profit curve in the second-price auction is a smooth peak at your value, not a flat line with cliffs: only the single-round counterfactual shows a flat price.

ideas.title: Cron Daylight Saving Checker
ideas.plainSentence: A checker that lets you enter a cron line and a time zone and see which runs vanish or double on the two daylight-saving nights.
ideas.pitch: The visitor enters a five-field cron line and picks an IANA time zone. The page draws the spring-forward and fall-back nights as a minute timeline and marks every run under two named rules: the literal wall-clock rule in crontab(5) (skipped time never fires, repeated time fires twice) and the classic cron(8) rule (a skipped fixed-time job fires right after the jump, a repeated one fires once). Each run shows local time, UTC and offset, so a nightly 02:30 job is seen vanishing in New York in March, and a 01:30 job running twice in November under the literal rule. It runs offline from the browser's zone data, with no account or upload, and prints its limits.
ideas.firstMinute: The page opens with a sample line (30 2 * * *) in America/New_York and the March spring-forward night already drawn: the 02:30 run is marked as lost under the wall-clock rule and as run at 03:00 under the classic rule. One click on the fall-back tab shows the 01:30 run counted twice versus once, so the first success needs no reading.
conceptsToLearn: A cron line has five fields: minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week
ideas.whyNow: Clocks go back in the EU and UK on 2026-10-25 and in the US on 2026-11-01, so people with nightly jobs are about to meet the repeated hour; the tool stays useful every spring and autumn.

purposeDetail.job: Show what a five-field cron line does on the two clock-change nights of one IANA zone, under two named scheduler rules, with local time, UTC and offset for every run.
purposeDetail.audience: Developers, sysadmins and data engineers with nightly or hourly jobs who need to know whether a job will be lost or doubled at a daylight-saving change, without trusting a next-runs list that ignores the jump.

paywallEvidence.product: Pay-per-event cron parser listings on a cloud automation marketplace
paywallEvidence.whatIsGated: Metered calls that return next fire times, priced per expression; no listing seen draws the daylight-saving nights or compares scheduler rules

purposeDetail.freeGap: Free options already list next runs and some claim DST handling (fact 4). The real gap is that none seen draws the two clock-change nights as a timeline, compares the literal and the classic rule, shows its working per run, or works offline with no upload. This is not a paywalled job; the value is private, offline and explanatory, and the paywall claim never goes on the page.
purposeDetail.oracle: The crontab(5) and cron(8) manual pages (Linux man-pages and OpenBSD) for the two rules, applied to the published 2026 fall-back dates (EU and UK 2026-10-25, US 2026-11-01); each self-test vector names the rule and the date it comes from. Vectors for spring-forward nights are regression checks unless their dates are sourced.
purposeDetail.inputs: A five-field cron line (with lists, ranges, steps and month or weekday names), an IANA zone chosen from a bundled list, and a choice of year and of spring or fall night.
purposeDetail.outputs: A minute-level timeline of the chosen night, a table of every run with local time, UTC and offset under each rule, a one-line verdict (lost, doubled, shifted, unchanged), and a copyable plain-text report.
purposeDetail.limits: Dialects differ and the page cannot know which scheduler the visitor runs; it models two documented rules only. Not modelled: systemd timers, cloud schedulers, Quartz, jobs started late by a busy machine, and clock changes of three hours or more (which cron(8) treats as clock corrections). Zone data comes from the visitor's browser and may lag the newest tzdata release.

research.summary: The two named rules are real and documented separately. The Linux crontab(5) page says times that do not exist never match and times that occur twice run matching jobs twice; the cron(8) pages (OpenBSD, Debian cronie, NetBSD) say clock changes under three hours get special handling for fixed-time or longer-than-hourly jobs: skipped ones run immediately after a forward jump, repeated ones are not run twice, and more frequent jobs are scheduled normally. A FreeBSD bug report is titled as a contradiction between the two pages, and the Healthchecks author says their CronSim library follows Debian cron, which shows dialects differ and the tool should say so. Search results suggest free next-run testers do not draw the DST nights; that was not confirmed by opening any of them. The EU and UK change dates for 2026 are confirmed by two results.

ideas.title: How Puzzle Solvers Work
ideas.plainSentence: A lesson that lets you step a computer solver through tiling puzzles, undo its dead ends and count every solution, up to sudoku.
ideas.pitch: Watch a slow-motion solver tile small boards with dominoes and pentominoes, then take the controls: pick the next piece yourself, see the dead end, back up, and watch a counter tick up as every tiling is found. A glowing marker always points at the square with the fewest options, and you learn why that one rule tames the search. The last rung shows that sudoku is the same kind of problem, so a puzzle designer can ask 'does it have exactly one answer?' by counting to two.
ideas.firstMinute: A small board is already being tiled by a slow-motion solver: pieces drop in, a dead end appears, the pieces lift out, and a counter shows how many tilings have been found. A glowing marker sits on the square with the fewest options. The visitor presses Step to advance the solver and sees it hit a dead end, back up and find a full tiling, which is the first success.
conceptsToLearn: Covering a board exactly means every square is covered by exactly one piece: no gaps, no overlaps
ideas.whyNow: Timeless. The same small idea sits behind pentomino puzzles and sudoku solvers, and few people see that it is one idea.

purposeDetail.concept: Exact cover: choose from a list of allowed placements so that every square is covered exactly once, and how a backtracking solver finds, and counts, all the ways by always branching on the most constrained square.
purposeDetail.whyNiche: It is the hidden common core of pentomino tilings, sudoku, and scheduling puzzles, yet most people meet it only as 'a clever linked-list trick'. Seeing the table of placements makes the trick obvious.
purposeDetail.audience: Curious puzzle fans, students meeting backtracking, and anyone who has wondered how a sudoku solver can prove a puzzle has only one answer.
misconceptions: A puzzle solver just tries every combination until one works (a natural first guess).
Tiling puzzles and sudoku are unrelated families of puzzle (a natural first guess).
purposeDetail.ahaMoment: Re-draw the board as a table where each row is one legal placement and each column is one thing that must be covered once; solving is just picking rows with exactly one tick in every column. Then the same table solves a sudoku.
demos: Rung 1: slow-motion solver tiling a small board with dominoes; step, undo, and a counter of tilings found
Rung 2: you pick pieces by hand and the page lights the beacon on the tightest square; compare your tries with the solver's
Rung 3: the table view, rows as placements and columns as squares, with choose, cover and undo highlighted
Rung 4: a board with two opposite corners removed, where the solver proves zero tilings; and the 6 by 10 pentomino board counted live against the published total
Rung 5: sudoku redrawn as the same table, and 'count to two' as a uniqueness check on a puzzle the visitor edits
checkQuestions: If a square has zero legal placements left, what must the solver do, and why is that good news for speed?
Why does picking the square with the fewest options first usually shrink the search?
A sudoku solver finds one answer. What else must it check before saying the puzzle has exactly one?
In the table view, what does it mean when a column has no rows left?

research.summary: Re-checked by search only. Knuth's Dancing Links paper (arXiv) presents Algorithm X as a recursive depth-first backtracking search, uses pentomino placement as its worked example, notes that the choice of which item to branch on matters, and reports 2339 essentially different tilings of the 6 by 10 rectangle; a lecture-notes paper agrees on 2339 excluding rotations and reflections of the whole board. A second paper applies Algorithm X to pentominoes, Latin squares and sudoku. The 17-clue minimum for a one-answer sudoku was found in one attributed result and stays flagged, as do the Norvig essay and the 729 by 324 counts, which the page derives from the rules. The two named misconceptions are natural first guesses, not documented beliefs.

facts.claim: Pentomino tilings and sudoku are both worked as exact cover problems, and Knuth's Algorithm X is a recursive depth-first backtracking search that finds all solutions; Dancing Links is its fast implementation.
Knuth's Dancing Links paper uses pentomino placement as its worked example, with each possible placement of a piece as one row of the table.

The 6 by 10 rectangle can be tiled by the 12 pentominoes in 2339 essentially different ways, counting rotations and reflections of the whole board as the same (so 4 times 2339 = 9356 raw tilings, computed).

Knuth's paper stresses that the choice of which item to branch on strongly affects speed (branch where something is hardest to fill); the page measures the effect of branching on the fewest-options square on its own boards, computed.

Derived from the rules, not quoted: sudoku as exact cover has 9 times 9 times 9 = 729 candidate placements and 4 times 81 = 324 things to cover once (cells, row-digit, column-digit and box-digit pairs).

A sudoku designer rung: edit clues and the solver counts to two, reporting none, one or several answers

Cut: free-form piece editor, other polyominoes, speed race. If time runs short the table-view animation shrinks to a static highlighted table, and rung 4's mutilated board stays as a single preset.
risks: The 729 and 324 sudoku counts are derived from the rules by the page and shown as derived, not as a sourced figure.
The 2339 figure counts tilings up to rotating or flipping the whole board; the page says so and labels the raw total it finds (9356) as computed.

Counting all tilings of the 6 by 10 board live must stay fast; builders time it, run it in a worker (the page shell allows blob workers), and fall back to counting the 3 by 20 board or showing a progress bar if it is slow.
The 17-clue minimum rests on one attributed result and shows as 'as of 2026-10-13, per the encyclopedia article on the mathematics of sudoku', or is omitted.
The Norvig essay and tutorial pages were not found again; the page cites Knuth's paper for the branching rule and shows its own measured node counts.
The two misconceptions are natural first guesses, not documented beliefs; the page words them as 'a natural first guess' and cites no survey.
The mutilated-board claim (zero tilings with two opposite corners removed) is computed by the page and labelled computed.
Risk of being too abstract: board view first, table view second, plain sentence in the intro's first line; the term 'exact cover' is introduced only after the first success.

A single generic solver with five rungs is buildable in a morning, and the misconceptions are honest first guesses, not documented beliefs.

ideas.title: Why Flat Maps Distort
ideas.plainSentence: A lesson that lets you drag countries on a world map and watch their size change, to see why flat maps always distort something.
ideas.pitch: Drag Greenland down a Mercator map and watch it shrink beside Africa, then switch to other projections with Tissot's circles drawn on them and plot a flight that is curved on one map and straight on another. A ladder of five small demos with check-yourself questions tests the assumption that one map is the true one and ends on the point that every map is an argument. Made for travellers and geography fans, no maths needed, all offline.
ideas.firstMinute: The page opens on a Mercator world map where a ghost-ember copy of Greenland already slides toward Africa and shrinks, with the caption that it is the same country with the same true area. The visitor drags Greenland themself and sees a live 'drawn size vs true size' readout fall to 1x at the equator. No reading is needed for that first success.
conceptsToLearn: A map is a flat picture of a ball, so some stretching is unavoidable
Drawn size versus true size is a ratio: 1x means the country is drawn at its real size
ideas.whyNow: Timeless: the Greenland-versus-Africa picture is a perennial geography topic and a hot spot for a classroom assumption about map sizes. Nothing on the page depends on the date.

purposeDetail.concept: A sphere cannot be flattened without distorting something. A projection chooses what to keep: Mercator keeps angles (conformal) and so stretches lengths by sec(latitude) and areas by sec squared (4 times at 60 degrees, about 33 times at 80); equal-area maps keep area and bend shapes; no projection can be both conformal and equal-area; great circles are straight only on a gnomonic map.
purposeDetail.whyNiche: Usual explanations are either a static 'Mercator is bad' infographic or a true-size drag toy with no why: nobody shows the area-scale curve, the Tissot circles and the great-circle flight together, or says that Mercator is excellent at its actual job (straight compass courses).
purposeDetail.audience: Curious travellers, geography fans, students and anyone who has argued about Greenland on a world map.
prerequisites: what latitude and longitude are, roughly
misconceptions: The wall-map (Mercator) shows true country sizes.
There is one correct projection and the others are wrong.
The straight line drawn on a map is the shortest route.
purposeDetail.ahaMoment: Dragging the same Tissot circle from the equator to the Arctic: on Mercator it stays round but swells to many times its size, on the equal-area map it keeps its size but flattens into an ellipse, and you realise you can never keep both.
demos: Rung 1: drag Greenland (and any country) across a Mercator map with a live drawn-size-over-true-size readout and a ghost showing home size.
Rung 2: the stretch dial: slide a latitude marker and see the sec-squared area multiplier (1x, 2x at 45 degrees, 4x at 60, about 33x at 80, computed) beside a row of identical true-size circles.

Rung 3: Tissot's circles on a gallery of five projections (Mercator, plain equirectangular, equal-area cylindrical, sinusoidal, azimuthal) with a shape-error and area-error meter showing that no map zeroes both.
Rung 4: pick two cities and fly the shortest route: curved on Mercator, straight on a gnomonic view, with the constant-compass-heading line (rhumb line) for contrast.
Rung 5: 'argue with a map': match jobs (sailing course, country sizes, polar flights) to the projection that serves them.
checkQuestions: On a Mercator map, by about what factor is the area of a small shape at 60 degrees latitude exaggerated? (4)
Greenland is about what fraction of South America's real area? (about one eighth; Mercator draws it larger)
On an equal-area map, what happens to a Tissot circle near the edge? (same area, becomes an ellipse)
What does a great-circle flight look like on a gnomonic map? (a straight line)
Why can't a map be both equal-area and conformal? (a sphere cannot be flattened keeping both angles and areas true)

research.summary: Re-checked by search only. PROJ's own documentation says Mercator is conformal, draws rhumb lines straight, is poor for world maps, and shows Greenland larger than South America though it is about one eighth of its area. Several results agree great circles are straight only on a gnomonic map and that Mercator straight lines are rhumb lines. Four results agree on Tissot behaviour (circles stay round but change size on conformal maps, keep area but become ellipses on equal-area maps). A sphere cannot be mapped both conformally and equal-area; the sec-squared area multipliers are derived by the page. Africa about 14 times Greenland and the belief that wall maps show true sizes rest on weak or informal sources, so they stay flagged.

facts.claim: PROJ's documentation says Mercator is conformal, draws rhumb lines (constant heading) as straight lines, and is poor for world maps because the projected area of Greenland looks larger than South America's although it is about one eighth of it.
Great circles are straight lines on a gnomonic projection, while on Mercator the straight lines are rhumb lines and most great circles are curved.
On conformal maps (Mercator) Tissot circles stay circles but change size; on equal-area maps they keep their area but become ellipses of varying shape.
No map projection can be both equal-area and conformal (a result tied to Gauss's Theorema Egregium; the Euler attribution is secondary).

Derived, not quoted: Mercator's linear scale is sec(latitude) in every direction, so area scales by sec squared: 4.00 at 60 degrees, 8.55 at 70 and 33.16 at 80 (computed here). The page computes these; builders check the formulas against Snyder's USGS Working Manual.

The belief that wall maps show true country sizes is described in informal essays and an education article, not in a controlled study; unverified by my search and shown only as a commonly raised assumption.

As of 2026-10-13, several search results put Africa at roughly 14 times Greenland's area (about 30.2 versus 2.17 million square km); the entries were not individually attributed, so the page shows 'about' and uses its own bundled outlines.

ideas.title: Priority Inversion Lesson
ideas.plainSentence: A lesson that shows, on draggable task timelines, how a low-priority task holding a lock can stall an urgent one, and what fixes it.
ideas.pitch: In 1997 the Mars Pathfinder spacecraft kept resetting because a lock was held by the wrong task at the wrong time, and the fix was a single setting. This lesson replays that bug on a three-task timeline, lets the visitor stretch one task and see the urgent one wait longer and longer, then flips on priority inheritance and watches it recover. A last rung compares a binary semaphore with a mutex.
ideas.firstMinute: The first frame already shows three coloured task lanes over time, with the urgent task blocked behind a lock and a red 'reset' marker where its deadline passes. A toggle labelled priority inheritance sits beside it; flipping it replays the same schedule and the urgent task finishes on time. No reading is needed to see the before and after.
conceptsToLearn: A lock lets only one task use shared data at a time, so others wait
ideas.whyNow: Timeless: the 1997 Pathfinder resets are a standard teaching case, documented first-hand by the mission's software lead. Not news-bound.

purposeDetail.concept: Priority inversion: when tasks share a lock and are scheduled by priority, a low-priority lock holder can be preempted by medium-priority work, so the urgent task waits for the medium one without ever sharing its lock; priority inheritance boosts the holder while it blocks someone more urgent.
purposeDetail.whyNiche: Most explanations of locks stop at 'only one at a time'. Priority inversion is the part that sinks real-time systems, and the mutex versus binary semaphore difference only makes sense once the visitor has seen it.
purposeDetail.audience: Curious programmers and students who have used locks or heard 'mutex vs semaphore' and want the picture, plus anyone who likes engineering failure stories.
prerequisites: A lock lets one task at a time use shared data
misconceptions: A binary semaphore is just a mutex with a count of one (a common shortcut that RTOS tutorials correct).
A lock can only delay an urgent task by the length of the other task's critical section (without inheritance the delay is uncontrolled).
purposeDetail.ahaMoment: Stretching the medium-priority task, which never touches the lock, and watching the urgent task's wait grow with it; then switching inheritance on and seeing the wait shrink to just the lock holder's short section.
demos: Two tasks, one lock: the second waits (the only prerequisite concept).
Three tasks by priority with a shared lock: the bug replays, the urgent task misses its deadline and a watchdog marker fires.
Stretch the medium task: the urgent task's wait grows without limit.
Switch priority inheritance on: the holder is boosted, the wait is only its critical section.
Switch to a priority ceiling and to a plain binary semaphore: see which protects and which does not boost.
checkQuestions: Which task runs while the urgent one waits, and why does it not need the lock?
With inheritance on, what priority does the lock holder run at while the urgent task is blocked on it?
Why does a signalling semaphore not give the holder a boost?
What is the longest the urgent task can now wait?

research.summary: The 1997 Pathfinder reset story is documented first-hand by a JPL software lead (a Dr. Dobb's article and a mailing-list message copied on a course page) and retold by a student blog: a low-priority task held a lock a high-priority bus task needed, medium-priority work kept preempting the holder, a watchdog forced resets, and the fix was enabling the lock's priority-inheritance option, sent to the spacecraft remotely. The formal result comes from the 1990 Sha, Rajkumar and Lehoczky paper (abstract and lecture notes seen): ordinary primitives allow uncontrolled inversion, inheritance and ceiling protocols fix it, and the ceiling protocol bounds blocking to one critical section and prevents deadlock. RTOS tutorials agree that mutexes have an owner and priority inheritance while binary semaphores are for signalling, with the boundary depending on the API. Reddit was not reachable, so no forum thread was seen.

facts.claim: In the 1997 Mars Pathfinder resets, a low-priority task held a lock needed by a high-priority bus task, medium-priority work kept preempting the holder, a watchdog forced system resets, and the fix enabled the lock's priority-inheritance flag, uplinked to the spacecraft.

Sha, Rajkumar and Lehoczky (IEEE Transactions on Computers, 1990): direct use of ordinary synchronisation primitives can cause uncontrolled priority inversion; basic priority inheritance and the priority ceiling protocol both solve it, and the ceiling protocol bounds blocking to one critical section of a lower-priority task and prevents deadlock.

RTOS tutorials distinguish a mutex (has an owner, supports priority inheritance, for mutual exclusion) from a binary semaphore (no owner, for signalling between tasks and interrupts); the boundary is API-specific, so the page teaches intent and not a universal rule.
Under basic priority inheritance a lock holder runs at the priority of the highest-priority task blocked on it while it holds the lock (the mechanism the Pathfinder fix switched on).

design.coreLoop: Demo, question, aha: each rung is one fixed-priority timeline the visitor edits (task length, lock on or off, inheritance on or off), predicts the outcome for the urgent task, then sees it replay step by step. Check questions follow the rungs.

ideas.title: Great-Circle Route Calculator
ideas.plainSentence: A calculator that lets you compare the shortest route between two places with the straight-line map course, with distances and headings.
ideas.pitch: Pick two places from a bundled list or type coordinates, and see the great-circle distance, the constant-heading (rhumb line) distance, the extra distance the straight-on-the-map course costs, and how the compass heading changes along the shortest route. Two small maps show the same trip on Mercator and on a gnomonic view, and the waypoints (every N km) can be copied as a plain list. Everything runs in the browser and shows its formulas.
ideas.firstMinute: The page opens with a sample trip, Los Angeles airport (LAX) to Tokyo Narita (NRT), already computed here on a sphere: about 8,754 km along the great circle against about 9,236 km along the constant-heading course, roughly 5.5 percent more. Both routes are drawn on the Mercator map, and the visitor swaps either end to see the numbers change instantly.
conceptsToLearn: great circle: the shortest path between two points on a sphere
rhumb line: a path that keeps one compass heading, a straight line on a Mercator map
ideas.whyNow: Timeless utility for travellers, pilots-in-training, sailors and trivia lovers; it pairs with the map-distortion lesson but works alone.

purposeDetail.job: Compute, for any two points on Earth, the great-circle distance and bearings, the rhumb-line distance and constant bearing, the percentage penalty of the rhumb line, and evenly spaced waypoints along either path.
purposeDetail.audience: Travellers curious why flights curve, student pilots and sailors learning route planning, teachers, trivia and map fans.
purposeDetail.freeGap: Free tools already do the core job: a map-click nautical calculator with distances and bearings, free spreadsheets with waypoints, a free lite desktop program. No paywall is claimed. The remaining gap: private and offline, every formula shown with numbers, side-by-side Mercator and gnomonic pictures, an honest sphere-error note. The page names no product.
purposeDetail.oracle: Exact identities on a sphere of radius 6371 km (stated on the page): quarter meridian = pi/2 times R = 10007.54 km; one equatorial degree of longitude = 111.195 km; antipodes = pi times R = 20015.09 km; a rhumb along a parallel = cos(latitude) times longitude difference times R; rhumb equals great circle along a meridian. Computed by script. Worked pair LAX to NRT: 8,754 km great circle (two sites), 9,236 km rhumb (one site, plus my computation).
purposeDetail.inputs: Two places (a bundled list of about 60 cities with coordinates rounded to 0.1 degree, or typed latitude and longitude in decimal degrees), waypoint spacing, radius fixed at 6371 km.
purposeDetail.outputs: Distances in km, miles and nautical miles; initial, final and rhumb bearings; percent penalty; midpoint; waypoint list as plain text rows; two small SVG maps.
purposeDetail.limits: Spherical Earth only, so distances can be off by up to about 0.3 percent; no land, airspace, weather or wind; not for navigation; antimeridian paths wrap longitude; the gnomonic view cannot show points more than 90 degrees from its centre; city coordinates are rounded centres, so airport pairs differ (city centres give 8,819 km for Los Angeles to Tokyo, not 8,754).

research.summary: The method is textbook: haversine for great-circle distance, the initial-bearing formula and the isometric-latitude formula for rhumb lines. The reference-script author's own page says a spherical model typically errs by up to about 0.3 percent. A rhumb line is straight on a Mercator chart and a great circle is straight on a gnomonic chart, which navigators use to plan routes. Free tools already compute both (a map-click calculator, spreadsheets, a free lite program), so no paywall is claimed. Los Angeles airport to Tokyo Narita is about 8,754 km by great circle per two sites; the 9,236 km rhumb figure is from one site and matches my own computation, as do other pairs I computed.

ideas.title: Nonogram Puzzle Checker
ideas.plainSentence: A picture-by-numbers (nonogram) maker that lets you draw a picture, get its clues, and check whether it can be solved without guessing.
ideas.pitch: Draw a picture on a small grid and the page writes the number clues around it, like a picture-by-numbers puzzle. It then solves the puzzle the way a person would, one row or column at a time, and reports whether the clues have exactly one answer and whether the whole grid falls out without guessing. If it does not, it shades the stuck squares and suggests a one-square change that repairs it; then you print the puzzle sheet and an answer page.
ideas.firstMinute: A 10 by 10 sample picture is already drawn with its clues written around it, and a slow replay is solving it pass by pass in colour. A verdict card reads something like 'One answer, no guessing needed, 6 passes, easy'. Click a single square to flip it and watch the verdict change, perhaps to 'Two answers' with the ambiguous squares shaded.
conceptsToLearn: A nonogram is a picture-by-numbers grid: each number says how long a run of filled squares is in that row or column.
ideas.whyNow: Timeless: anyone who makes puzzles for a book, a class or a friend hits the same trap, a puzzle that has one answer on paper but forces guessing. The page makes that visible in seconds.

purposeDetail.job: Turn a drawn picture into nonogram clues and prove, with visible working, whether the puzzle has exactly one answer and can be finished by row-and-column logic alone.
purposeDetail.audience: Puzzle makers, teachers, parents and hobbyists who want to design nonograms that are fair to solve, and solvers curious why a puzzle got stuck.

paywallEvidence.product: A paid no-guess nonogram toolkit sold through a small-seller storefront
paywallEvidence.whatIsGated: The check that every accepted puzzle can be finished by row-and-column logic alone, plus a print-ready puzzle-book PDF with answer pages; listed at 29 US dollars as of 2026-10-13, per the seller's own listing (never shown on the page).

purposeDetail.freeGap: Free options check uniqueness (a game's maker feature, open-source editors and solvers), so uniqueness alone is not the gap. I saw no free tool that tests the stricter no-guess property, shows each solving pass and proposes a one-square repair, but that is unconfirmed. The remaining gap: private, in the browser, shows its working, suggests the fix. The page names no product.
purposeDetail.oracle: OEIS A391619: the number of n by n grids with a unique solution reachable by row-and-column logic alone is 1, 2, 14, 384, 51234 for sizes 0 to 4 and 24976511 for size 5. The self-test enumerates every grid up to 4 by 4 and compares; the 5 by 5 count is an optional background run. The newsletter's stuck 5 by 5 puzzle is a further case.
purposeDetail.inputs: A picture drawn by clicking or dragging on a grid from 5 by 5 to 15 by 15 (20 by 20 under More), or pasted clue numbers; a sample picture is preloaded.
purposeDetail.outputs: Clue numbers, a verdict (no solution, several solutions, one solution needing guesses, or one solution reached by logic alone), a difficulty label from the pass count, the stuck squares, a suggested one-square repair, and exports: puzzle sheet and answer page as PNG, SVG and a print layout, plus a share link holding the grid.
purposeDetail.limits: Black-and-white nonograms only, 5 to 15 squares a side. Exhaustive checking of larger grids is capped and reported as 'could not decide' rather than guessed. Difficulty is a rough label from solving passes, not a verdict on how hard a person will find it. No photo import.

research.summary: Uniqueness and no-guess solvability are different properties. A seller of a paid toolkit says most nonogram generators check nothing or only uniqueness, while its own accepted puzzles must be finished by working one row or column at a time (seller claim). OEIS A391619 counts n by n grids that are unique and line-solvable (1, 2, 14, 384, 51234, 24976511 for sizes 0 to 5), and the 5 by 5 value is also reported by a puzzle newsletter and a forum thread. A larger unique-solution count for 5 by 5 was relayed by a commenter and is unverified. facts.claim: As of 2026-10-13 a seller's own listing offers a no-guess nonogram toolkit for 29 US dollars. It says a puzzle is accepted only if working one row or column at a time, filling only forced squares, finishes the grid, and that most generators check nothing or only uniqueness (seller claim).
A nonogram can have exactly one solution and still not be solvable by row-and-column logic alone; a puzzle newsletter gives a small 5 by 5 example where line work gets stuck.
Of the 33,554,432 possible 5 by 5 grids, 24,976,511 give puzzles that are unique and solvable by line logic alone; OEIS A391619 lists 1, 2, 14, 384, 51234, 24976511 for sizes 0 to 5.

Deciding whether a nonogram has a solution is NP-complete (Ueda and Nagao, 1996), and deciding uniqueness of a given solution is also hard, so an exhaustive answer count on large grids needs a work cap; simple nonograms are solved by cheap local line reasoning.

A free game's maker feature uses a solver that rejects puzzles with several solutions, and open-source nonogram editors and solvers exist; no free tool seen in my searches tests the stricter no-guess property with a repair suggestion (not confirmed for every tool).

ideas.title: Poker Chips Aren't Dollars
ideas.plainSentence: A lesson that lets you drag poker tournament stacks and prizes to see why chips are not worth their share of the prize money.
ideas.pitch: Why would anyone fold a big hand near the money? This lesson answers it with a ladder of live demos: set the stacks and prizes, watch chip share and prize-money share drift apart, then test a bubble all-in and see the extra winning chance a call needs. Every number is computed in the page and the sum is shown step by step, with simulated chips only and no real money.
ideas.firstMinute: The first frame already shows three stacks and a 50/30/20 prize split, with a bar for each player's chip share beside a bar for the prize money the model gives them (the 50% stack gets about 38%). Sliding any stack makes both bars move at once, so the gap is seen before any text is read. A one-line caption names the gap, and that is the first success.
conceptsToLearn: A tournament pays prizes by finishing place, not by how many chips you hold
ideas.whyNow: Timeless: the question of why chips are not worth their face value near the money is a standard one in tournament poker teaching, and the answer is a short sum that few explainers let you move. Not news-bound. A claim that discussion forums ask it every week is unverified (the forum site could not be searched) and stays off the page.

purposeDetail.concept: The independent chip model: a way to turn each player's chips into expected prize money, by treating finishing order as repeated draws where each remaining player is picked in proportion to chips. It shows why chip value is not linear in dollars.
purposeDetail.whyNiche: Everyone has heard that you fold aces on the bubble, almost nobody has moved the numbers. Most explainers state one worked example; this one lets the visitor change stacks, prizes and the all-in and see each sum.
purposeDetail.audience: Curious non-experts and casual tournament players who want to understand why 'a chip is a chip' fails in a prize-ladder game. No poker-hand knowledge needed.
prerequisites: A tournament pays prizes by finishing place
misconceptions: Doubling your chips doubles what they are worth in prize money.
A player with half the chips owns half the prize pool.
purposeDetail.ahaMoment: Moving a slider so one stack doubles and watching its prize-money bar rise by far less than double, while the short stacks gain without risking a chip.
demos: Winner-take-all with two players: chips equal dollars exactly, the one case where the common belief holds.
Three players, 50/30/20 split: drag stacks and compare chip share bars with prize-money bars, with the finishing-order table shown.
The double-up: one stack doubles by taking chips from another and the prize-money gain is compared with the chip gain.

The bubble all-in: pick two stacks and a call, and see the winning chance a call needs under chip counting versus under the model, and the gap between them (dead money in the pot is left out and said so).
Where the model is only an approximation: skill, blinds and position are ignored, with a plain list of limits.
checkQuestions: If the prize ladder were flat (everyone paid the same), what would a chip be worth?
Why does the short stack's prize share exceed its chip share?
A medium stack faces an all-in from a bigger stack: does the required winning chance go up or down compared with chip counting, and why?
What does the model leave out that a real table has?

research.summary: The idea is a real, recurring poker-discussion question (why chips are worth less than face value near the money). The model is documented in a university course lecture (MIT OpenCourseWare 15.S50 lecture 6) and many strategy guides; its mechanics (finishing probability proportional to chips, remove the winner, repeat) are the Harville procedure from horse-racing statistics. I reproduced a published 3-player example (500/300/200 chips, 50/30/20 prizes of 100) exactly in a script: 38.39, 32.75, 28.86, but only one guide's numbers were seen (flagged unverified), and another guide's similar example shows about 42% for the big stack, so published figures do not agree and the page must compute and show its own sum. Free browser ICM calculators for final tables already exist, so this is a lesson, not a paywall-clone tool. Search could not reach Reddit, so the brief's thread claim is unconfirmed.

facts.claim: MIT OpenCourseWare 15.S50 (How to Win at Texas Hold'em, IAP 2016) has a Lecture 6 on the independent chip model, which says tournament chip value is nonlinear in prize money and contrasts it with chip-EV play, treated as an approximation; a betting-site guide also says doubling a stack does not double its equity.

Reported procedure behind ICM (Harville): the chance a player finishes first is their chips divided by all chips; remove that player, renormalise to get second place, and so on; equity is the sum of place probability times prize. Not re-found by this pass, so the page presents it as the model's definition and shows the sums.

Reported worked example (as of 2026-10-13, per VIP-Grinders): stacks 500/300/200 with prizes 50/30/20 of 100 give 38.39, 32.75 and 28.86. A script using the procedure above reproduced 38.3929, 32.75 and 28.8571 (a regression check, not an independent oracle).
Reported (unverified, per VIP-Grinders): free browser ICM calculators for final tables of 2 to 9 players exist, so the page makes no paywall claim and does not name any calculator.

Reported (unverified, per a Berkeley statistics paper): Harville-type models misestimate second and third place chances in horse-racing data, so ICM is an approximation; the page lists what the model leaves out as its own assumptions (finishing order is driven by chip counts only).

sophisticationHooks: Exact enumeration of finishing orders for up to 9 players with the full probability-by-place table shown, no sampling.
Required-winning-chance readout for a bubble all-in: (equity now minus equity if lost) divided by (equity if won minus equity if lost), compared with the chip-counting break-even.
Honest limits panel and a note that published worked examples disagree, with this page's sums shown for checking by hand.
design.scopeForOneDay: Built: 5 rungs, one pure ICM function (exact enumeration, up to 6 players on sliders and 9 in the table, any prize list), an all-in required-equity function, a shown-working table, 4 check questions, and a node self-check for 2-player winner-take-all, 3-player 500/300/200 and equal-prize cases plus one hand-checked all-in. Cut: tournament simulation, hand ranges, blinds, multi-table, saved progress. Plenty of slack for QA at this size.
risks: Unverified claim: that discussion forums ask this question every week. The forum site could not be searched, so the page names no thread or user and does not state the claim.
Unverified claim: the published 38.39/32.75/28.86 example. The page says computed here, shows its sum, and quotes a published figure only as 'as of 2026-10-13, per VIP-Grinders' or omits it.

Unverified claims: the Harville procedure source, the approximation-in-horse-racing remark and the free-calculator claim. The page defines the model itself, never names a calculator, and treats the horse-racing remark as omitted.
ICM is an approximation (skill, blinds and position ignored); the page states this, avoids advice wording, uses simulated chips only and says estimates, not advice.
Free calculators may exist; differentiation is the teaching ladder and shown working, so the page stays a lesson and not a calculator.
The all-in required-chance formula ignores dead money, chops and later hands: define it exactly in the spec and check it by hand on one case in the node self-check.
Rung 4 and the up-to-9-player enumeration are the heaviest parts; if time runs short, cap the sliders at 6 players and keep exact enumeration.

ideas.title: Gains From Trade Lesson
ideas.plainSentence: A lesson where you set two neighbours' working hours and find a swap that leaves both better off, even if one is better at everything.
ideas.pitch: Two neighbours split their working day between quilts and fish, and one of them is faster at both. You set each one's hours with a slider, see the pair's total output, then try to find a swap that leaves both with more. The page shows the opportunity cost behind it, the range of exchange rates that works for both sides, and what the stronger side misses by refusing to trade.
ideas.firstMinute: The first frame shows a table of hours needed per item for two neighbours and a small quilt-like grid of their output, with a sample swap already done. You nudge one slider and watch both totals update; a banner says who now has more of what, and the first success is finding a swap where both columns grow.
conceptsToLearn: opportunity cost: what you give up to make one more of something
ideas.whyNow: Timeless; useful for anyone who argues about trade, outsourcing or who should do which chore.

purposeDetail.concept: A party has a comparative advantage in a good when its opportunity cost of making it is lower than its partner's. Even if one party needs fewer hours for everything (an absolute advantage in both), the two have different opportunity costs, so each specialising where its cost is lower and swapping at a rate between the two costs leaves both with more of both goods.
purposeDetail.whyNiche: The idea is taught as a conclusion and tangled with absolute advantage, so learners assume the stronger side has nothing to gain. Textbooks give one worked table; few let you search for the swap yourself.
purposeDetail.audience: Curious adults, students, and anyone who argues about trade or outsourcing.
misconceptions: A person or country that is better at everything gains nothing from trading with a weaker partner.
Comparative advantage and absolute advantage mean the same thing.
purposeDetail.ahaMoment: You see the stronger neighbour's own opportunity cost for fishing is higher than the weaker neighbour's, because every hour on fish is an hour not spent on the quilt it makes faster; the swap that fits between the two costs leaves both with more.
demos: Rung 1: absolute advantage table with sliders for hours; total output before trade.
Rung 2: the same table turned into opportunity costs; the page shows the cost of one quilt in fish for each neighbour.
Rung 3: find the swap yourself by dragging the exchange rate; a green band shows the range where both gain and red shows where one loses.
Rung 4: the stronger neighbour refuses to trade, then trades at a rate inside the range, and the page compares the two outcomes (for example 2.5 quilts for 2.5 fish).
Rung 5: change the table so both costs are equal and watch the gains vanish; then explain why.
Rung 6: checks with new numbers drawn from the textbook-style examples.
checkQuestions: Neighbour A needs 2 hours per quilt and 3 hours per fish. What does one quilt cost A in fish? (two thirds of a fish)
Neighbour B needs 6 hours per quilt and 4 hours per fish. Who has the comparative advantage in fish? (B)
Can a swap at one fish per quilt help both? (yes, it lies between 2/3 and 3/2)
If both neighbours had the same opportunity cost, would trade create gains? (no)

research.summary: Textbooks define comparative advantage through opportunity cost and warn that absolute advantage alone is incomplete; OpenStax, a publisher of free textbooks, states this on its own page, and study guides and glossaries list confusing the two as a common error. The page's own two-neighbour table is hand-checked: with 24 working hours each, neighbour A needs 2 hours per quilt and 3 per fish, B needs 6 and 4. Before trade A makes 6 quilts and 4 fish and B makes 2 and 3 (totals 8 and 7). At A 9 quilts and 2 fish and B 6 fish the totals are 9 and 8, and swapping 2.5 quilts for 2.5 fish at one fish per quilt leaves A with 6.5 and 4.5 and B with 2.5 and 3.5, strictly more of both. This is my own regression check, not an oracle. A claim that complete specialisation is a misreading is single-source and flagged.

facts.claim: A country has a comparative advantage in a good when its opportunity cost of making it is lower than its partner's; absolute advantage compares inputs per unit, and trade rests on comparative advantage rather than absolute advantage alone.
Study guides and glossaries list confusing comparative advantage with absolute advantage as a common error.
Specialising along comparative advantage can raise total output from unchanged resources, so both sides can gain even when one is better at making both goods.
Increasing opportunity costs and other real-world limits make complete specialisation unlikely; the lesson's constant-cost table is a classroom simplification (one study guide only, flagged).

inspirations: the lawyer and her typist example

design.coreLoop: Demo, question, aha: set hours on the sliders, see total output and each side's opportunity cost, drag the exchange rate to find the range where both gain, answer a check question, then change the table and repeat.
sophisticationHooks: A green and red band on the exchange-rate slider computed from the two opportunity costs.
A stronger-neighbour-refuses scenario that compares outcomes with and without trade.
An equal-costs table where gains vanish, proving the cause is the cost difference.
A built-in test that recomputes every number on the page from the table.
design.scopeForOneDay: Build: three production tables (the hand-checked 24-hour one, a textbook-style one, a trap with equal costs), SVG quilt-patch output grids, exchange-rate band, five or six rungs, check questions, explainer, a script check of every number against the table. The worked swap must give strictly more of both goods, for example 2.5 quilts for 2.5 fish. Cut: more than two goods or parties, money, tariffs and policy, who gains inside each country, complete-specialisation claims.
risks: The lesson is a simplified constant-cost two-good model; the page says so and makes no claims about real trade policy or about who gains and loses inside a country. Keep political: false and take no stance on tariffs.
The scout's swap of 3 quilts for 3 fish leaves A's quilts and B's fish unchanged, a weak gain; the builders use 2.5 for 2.5 or a table with strict gains in every column.

The complete-specialisation point rests on one study guide, and the Ricardo source and the Saylor and Econlib pages were not re-found; the page uses its own numbers, labels them as such and does not call complete specialisation a misconception.
A 2023 paper reportedly argues Ricardo's four numbers were not unit labour coefficients; no source was recorded, so the page does not claim to reproduce Ricardo's own numbers.
The sources are textbooks and study aids; the making-of panel lists the textbook first and avoids advocacy institutes where a textbook says the same.
Keep the first screen simple: at most 8 controls and the primary action visible at 1280x650.
